title: Isolations
summary: Anchor one staff end and circle the other around it, then explore the timing and plane variations.

setup.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
setup.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
setup.plane: Wall plane for the basic explanation; wall and wheel plane variants are demonstrated.

moves.name: Thumb-end isolation
moves.description: Keep the thumb-side tip near a single point on the body midline at about shoulder height while the other tip circles it.
moves.grip: Center grip; at the upper and lower positions let the shaft rest against the thumb joint with the fingers extending toward the pinky end.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: Watch the anchored end, not just the moving end.

steps.title: Choose the center
steps.body: Imagine a point halfway between the shoulders at shoulder height.

steps.title: Orbit the hand
steps.body: Move the hand around that point while continually aiming the thumb-side end at it.

steps.title: Accommodate the grip
steps.body: At the top and bottom, use the thumb-joint support demonstrated in the grip lesson.

steps.title: Check the anchor
steps.body: Use a mirror to see whether the chosen tip wanders away from the target.

moves.name: Pinky-end isolation
moves.description: Use the pinky-side tip as the stationary end of the isolation.
moves.grip: Center grip with a comfortable closed hold; track the pinky-side end rather than changing which end is named.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: Keep the same end anchored through the entire circle.

steps.title: Change the anchored end
steps.body: Place the pinky end at the imagined shoulder-height center.

steps.title: Circle around it
steps.body: Let the hand and thumb end travel around that center.

steps.title: Keep a comfortable hold
steps.body: Drex shows this version without the pronounced open-thumb positions of the thumb-end version.

moves.name: Together same isolations
moves.description: Move the hands around their circles in the same direction and phase.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: Both hands arrive at each corresponding compass position together.

steps.title: Establish one isolation
steps.body: Choose one end to anchor and make its small hand orbit consistent.

steps.title: Add the second hand
steps.body: Move the hands around their circles in the same direction and phase.

steps.title: Hold the shape
steps.body: Keep each selected end near its isolation center as the other end travels around.

moves.description: Mirror the hand circles in front of the body.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: Both hands reach the top and bottom together while traveling opposite directions.

geometry.handRadius: Equal to the distance from grip to the anchored tip in an ideal planar isolation. With a center grip this is half the staff length.
geometry.model: hand = center + radius*(cos(theta),sin(theta)); orient one staff endpoint back to center.
geometry.interpretation: This radius equality is derived from the fixed-end definition, not a numeric measurement supplied by Drex.

title: Extensions
summary: Use full arm reach to carry the staff around a large circle without pinning a tip.

moves.description: Carry the staff around with the arm at full reach, with the thumb-side end pointing away from the body center. No tip is required to stay pinned.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.

title: Antispin
summary: Counterrotate each shaft against its hand circle, using the thumb or pinky end as the horizontal reference.

setup.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
setup.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
setup.plane: Wall plane for the breakdown; the reference includes both wall and wheel plane together-opposite variations.

moves.name: Thumb-led four-petal antispin
moves.description: The hand and shaft rotate in opposite directions. In the thumb-led version the thumb-side tip travels along a horizontal line across the shoulders; the other tip travels up and down.
moves.grip: Center grip; at the upper and lower positions let the shaft rest against the thumb joint with the fingers extending toward the pinky end.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: At either side, the pinky end passes outside the elbow rather than into the elbow crease.

steps.title: Start below the center
steps.body: Hold the staff vertically in front with the thumb end up, using the thumb-joint support.

steps.title: Slide to the right
steps.body: Send the thumb end horizontally right. Keep the pinky end on the outer, bony side of the elbow.

steps.title: Return through the top
steps.body: Bring the thumb end back toward the center as the pinky end rises.

steps.title: Slide left and return
steps.body: Send the thumb end left with the pinky end outside the elbow, then let the pinky end descend to the starting position.

moves.name: Pinky-led four-petal antispin
moves.description: Exchange the roles of the ends so the pinky-side tip is the horizontal reference. This gives the complementary antispin grip path.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: At the side positions the thumb end approaches the inner elbow, unlike the thumb-led version.

steps.title: Prepare the lower position
steps.body: Drex begins with the thumb directed down and the pinky end outside the elbow.

steps.title: Send the pinky outward
steps.body: Extend the pinky-side tip along the horizontal line while the thumb end comes toward the elbow crease.

steps.title: Raise the thumb end
steps.body: Let the thumb end rise, then send the pinky end outward on the other side.

steps.title: Return below
steps.body: Lower the thumb end and recover the starting relationship with the pinky end outside the elbow.

pitfalls: For thumb-led antispin, letting the pinky end enter the elbow crease and trapping the next upward movement.
Mixing up the horizontal tracking end with whichever end happens to point inward at one moment.
Counting only one end when naming the double-ended staff four-petal pattern.
Learning only one grip-path version, which makes later changes between isolations and antispins harder.

evidence.observation: Drex contrasts clockwise staff rotation with counterclockwise hand movement from his perspective.
He calls the shown pattern four-petal for a staff and two-petal for a one-ended prop.
Thumb-in versus pinky-in is defined by which end forms the horizontal shoulder-line path.
The thumb-led breakdown starts below the center with the thumb end up.
He explicitly contrasts pinky end outside the elbow with an uncomfortable inside-elbow path.
The pinky-led breakdown begins and reverses which endpoint follows the horizontal line.
The slow reference begins with thumbs-in together-same.
Thumbs-in together-opposite wall plane is labeled.
Thumbs-in together-opposite wheel plane is labeled separately.
Thumbs-in split opposites is labeled.
The final reference overlay identifies pinkies-in split same.

limitations: These are source-informed teaching diagrams, not motion capture. Hand paths and shaft angles do not specify exact shoulder, elbow, wrist, or finger mechanics.
The straight endpoint lines are a teaching ideal. Drex notes that his vertical line is less consistent than the horizontal line.
End-to-end traces are not a measurement of elbow clearance; the source grip demonstrations remain necessary.

geometry.handRadius: For ideal straight endpoint lines, use grip-to-tip length as the hand-orbit radius.
geometry.model: With equal radii and shaft angle -theta, one endpoint is (2*r*cos(theta),0) and the other is (0,2*r*sin(theta)), up to phase/sign. Swap endpoint identity for the pinky-led version.
geometry.interpretation: The source explicitly supplies opposite rotation and horizontal/vertical endpoint paths. The equality and equations are an ideal geometric derivation.
geometry.traceNote: The four outward compass points use both staff ends. A single tracked end does not draw a conventional four-lobed poi flower.

steps.title: Return through the left

pitfalls: Taking the short counterrotating route, which produces antispin instead.

limitations: These are source-informed teaching diagrams, not motion capture. Hand paths and shaft angles do not specify exact shoulder, elbow, wrist, or finger mechanics.

steps.title: Compare an extension

pitfalls: Using the word opposite without identifying whether it describes the hands or the staffs.
Losing the horizontal and vertical relationships at the compass checkpoints.
Forcing the briefly demonstrated isolation/extension pairing to fit proportions it does not suit.
Assuming same-direction hand paths imply same-direction staff rotation.

evidence.observation: A hybrid is introduced as two dissimilar patterns, including the brief isolation/extension comparison.
Drex prefers the contrast of isolation or extension with antispin and develops the isolation example.
He shows that the pattern assignments can remain fixed or switch at a checkpoint.
Horizontal and vertical staff relationships at four compass points are the stated target.
He demonstrates hands going up together and coming down apart.
He explains that the four-petal antispin and isolation/extension rotate by equal amounts in equal time.
Together-same hybrid is named.
Together-opposite is explicitly described as the hands, not the staffs.
Split-opposite shows the parallel folding effect.
Split-same is demonstrated and compared with together-same.
The summary distinguishes same-direction hands/opposite staffs from opposite-direction hands/same staffs.

limitations: These are source-informed teaching diagrams, not motion capture. Hand paths and shaft angles do not specify exact shoulder, elbow, wrist, or finger mechanics.
The lesson suggests an extension/antispin alternative but gives the detailed compass breakdown with isolation/antispin.
The comparison with inspin is part of the preceding vocabulary; no separate inspin hybrid is developed here.

geometry.model: Combine a +1-turn isolation/extension shaft with a -1-turn antispin shaft. Assign each hand its own orbit direction and phase.
geometry.interpretation: Same-direction hands lead to opposite shaft rotation; opposite-direction hands lead to same shaft rotation for this pairing.
geometry.traceNote: Label hand arrows separately from shaft arrows. A single timing label cannot describe both.

title: R-types and chu-chus
summary: Keep one staff orientation fixed while its hand moves, then combine that translation with shoulder and hip reels.

moves.name: Upper chu-chu: shoulder reel plus R-type
moves.description: Use a shoulder reel in the upper hand while the lower staff keeps a vertical R-type orientation and follows the reel staff end.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: The lower staff thumb end tracks the upper staff pinky end; the upright R-type staff remains in front of the body.

steps.title: Stack the staffs
steps.body: Begin with one hand high and one low, both thumbs up. Align the upper pinky end with the lower thumb end.

steps.title: Rehearse the upper reel
steps.body: Drop the upper thumb end behind the back and bring the upper pinky end around to the front again.

steps.title: Add the follower
steps.body: Move the lower staff in an R-type so its thumb end follows the moving pinky end of the upper staff.

steps.title: Recover the stack
steps.body: Return to the upright end-to-end relationship in front of the body.

moves.name: Lower chu-chu: hip reel plus R-type
moves.description: Reverse the jobs: the lower hand performs the hip reel and the upper staff keeps its orientation while following the lower staff end.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: The upper pinky end tracks the lower thumb end; only the untracked end of the reel staff passes behind the body.

steps.title: Use the same home position
steps.body: Stack the two vertical staffs with both thumbs up.

steps.title: Rehearse the lower reel
steps.body: Send the lower pinky end outward, then behind the body and upward, before returning its thumb end to the top.

steps.title: Follow with the upper staff
steps.body: Keep the upper shaft upright and move its pinky end along the lower thumb-end path.

steps.title: Return in front
steps.body: Recover the stacked vertical position without sending the R-type staff behind the body.

moves.name: Alternating chu-chus
moves.description: Alternate the upper and lower reel roles whenever the staffs return to their shared upright home position.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: The home position is a decision point: one staff reels, the other remains an R-type follower.

steps.title: Perform the upper version
steps.body: Let the upper staff reel while the lower staff follows.

steps.title: Meet at home
steps.body: Return both staffs to the vertical front-body stack.

steps.title: Perform the lower version
steps.body: Let the lower staff reel while the upper staff follows.

steps.title: Repeat the exchange
steps.body: Alternate the roles through the common home position.

moves.name: Antispin plus R-type

steps.title: Choose the fixed staff
steps.body: Pick one hand to preserve an R-type orientation.

steps.title: Add antispin
steps.body: Give the other hand the familiar counterrotating four-petal path.

steps.title: Observe the contrast
steps.body: Keep the two movement rules distinct as they pass through the compass positions.

moves.name: Isolation plus R-type
moves.description: Pair an isolation with a translating, fixed-orientation staff.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.

steps.title: Anchor one endpoint
steps.body: Use an isolation with one hand.

steps.title: Translate the other staff
steps.body: Move the other hand around while its shaft angle stays unchanged.

steps.title: Compare the rules
steps.body: One staff turns about a stationary end; the other keeps its angle and moves both ends.

moves.name: Switching antispin and R-type roles
moves.description: Use antispin against R-type on the way up, then exchange the hand assignments at the top and continue downward. The demonstration requires two complete passes to recover the initial hand orientation.
moves.grip: Hold near the staff center and keep track of the thumb-side and pinky-side ends.
moves.stance: Stand comfortably facing the practice plane. Drex keeps his feet planted while his shoulders and elbows accommodate the movement; exact foot width is not prescribed.
moves.focus: Do not assume that one up-and-down pass returns the same grip orientation.

steps.title: Rise with unlike patterns
steps.body: Let one hand antispin while the other maintains an R-type.

steps.title: Exchange at the top
steps.body: Give the first hand the R-type job and the other the antispin job.

steps.title: Descend and repeat
steps.body: Continue down with the exchanged roles, then run the sequence again.

steps.title: Check the return
steps.body: Compare the hand and thumb orientations with the beginning after the second pass.

pitfalls: Rotating the supposedly fixed R-type shaft as the hand circles.
Sending the R-type staff behind the body in a chu-chu.
Following the wrong pair of ends: the linked relationship is upper pinky to lower thumb in the starting stack.
Switching chu-chu roles before returning to the shared upright front-body position.
Expecting one role-switching antispin/R-type pass to recover the starting hand orientation.

evidence.observation: Thumb-up fixed orientation is demonstrated, followed by pinky-up and palm-down/up choices.
Together-same and together-opposite R-type hand timing are briefly demonstrated.
The chu-chu setup places one hand high and one low, with both thumb ends up.
The upper shoulder reel is rehearsed before the lower R-type follower is added.
The lower thumb end is instructed to track the upper pinky end.
The bottom version changes to a hip reel.
The upper pinky end now tracks the lower thumb end.
Drex explicitly says the R-type staff remains in front; the untracked reel end passes behind.
He begins alternating top and bottom versions through the common home position.
Antispin versus R-type is offered as a further hybrid.
Isolation versus R-type is demonstrated next.
He switches antispin/R-type roles at the top and notes the need for two passes to restore hand orientation.

limitations: These are source-informed teaching diagrams, not motion capture. Hand paths and shaft angles do not specify exact shoulder, elbow, wrist, or finger mechanics.
The source calls for a point-of-contact relationship between tips; diagrams should portray a tracking relationship rather than instructing the learner to force physical impact.
The reel portion has depth and occlusion behind the body. A two-dimensional circle is insufficient to teach those mechanics.
The historical video-game aside is not necessary to perform the move and has not been independently checked.
Only together-same and together-opposite R-types receive explicit brief examples here; the source invites further timing exploration without separately teaching all four.

geometry.model: For R-types, translate the center around an orbit while keeping shaft angle fixed. For chu-chu, link one R-type endpoint to the visible tracked endpoint of a shoulder or hip reel.
geometry.interpretation: Fixed orientation is explicit in the source. Chu-chu needs a separate depth-aware mechanism or source-video checkpoint view, not the generic planar R-type alone.
